body:
## Summary

- add a deterministic build, pack, manifest, and verification harness for `@freeside/collection-protocol`
- bind package/schema/source identity and the complete compatibility fixture set to the artifact
- prove isolated clean-build byte reproducibility and exclude stale generated output
- provide one consumer-neutral verification entrypoint plus temporary CR-003/CR-105 legacy pin support

## Verification

- frozen install, typecheck, and package tests
- two isolated clean packs with byte-identical artifact and manifest
- seeded stale-output pack matches clean output
- artifact, manifest identity, fixture, version, and source-commit negative probes
- dependency-direction/cycle check
- legacy CR-003/CR-105 checksum verification
- independent reproducibility review

## Consumer follow-up

Sonar and Dashboard must pin the produced tarball plus manifest and run the shared verify-only entrypoint before install/tests. They must consume the package fixtures rather than fork schemas.

Tracks CR-005 in #472.

Draft only. Do not merge.

comments.body:
The collection protocol compatibility gate is green after the portable GNU/PAX precedence test amendment.

The remaining `agent-ci` failure is the existing repository baseline tracked in #477:

- per-user rate-limit behavior
- SSE drop recovery (`UND_ERR_SOCKET`)

Those failures reproduce outside this change and are unrelated to the collection protocol harness. No merge is requested; this remains a draft PR.

## Summary

Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES. This PR shows strong supply-chain instincts: isolated harness builds and archive preflight checks are exactly the right architectural direction. The remaining concerns are narrow but important: failure cleanup in CI and tar checksum validation are both boundary-integrity issues.

Compatibility harnesses are trust boundaries. The core question is not just “does this artifact pass?” but “can every actor in the path agree on what the artifact is?”

## Findings

<!-- bridge-findings-start -->
```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "findings": [
    {
      "id": "F-001",
      "title": "ci-compat can leave poisoned dist behind on failure",
      "severity": "MEDIUM",
      "category": "test-reliability",
      "file": "packages/protocol/collection/scripts/ci-compat.sh:98",
      "description": "The script appends a throwing export to dist/harness/pack.js and restores it only after pnpm run pack:artifact succeeds. With set -e, any failure in that command exits before the mv restore runs, leaving the checkout dist modified for the rest of the job or local run.",
      "suggestion": "Wrap the poison probe in a local trap or restore immediately via an ERR-safe cleanup function, similar to the try/finally pattern used in the Vitest version.",
      "confidence": 0.95,
      "faang_parallel": "Google's TAP-style test infrastructure treats cleanup as part of the test contract, not as best effort, because poisoned shared state causes misleading follow-on failures.",
      "metaphor": "This is like testing a smoke alarm by filling the kitchen with smoke, then only opening the windows if the test passes.",
      "teachable_moment": "Any test that mutates the checkout needs shell-level finally semantics. In bash, that usually means trap-based restoration before the risky command runs.",
      "connection": "This connects directly to hermetic testing: compatibility suites should fail closed, but they should not contaminate the next diagnostic step."
    },
    {
      "id": "F-002",
      "title": "Tar parser does not validate header checksums",
      "severity": "MEDIUM",
      "category": "security",
      "file": "packages/protocol/collection/src/harness/archive.ts:243",
      "description": "listTarGzipMembers parses 512-byte tar headers but never validates the tar header checksum before trusting name, typeflag, size, PAX, and GNU metadata. A corrupted or deliberately malformed archive can be interpreted by this parser before extraction tools reject or interpret it differently, weakening the pre-extract validation boundary.",
      "suggestion": "Compute and verify the tar checksum for each non-zero header block, accepting standard signed/unsigned variants as needed, and fail with ArtifactArchiveMismatch before reading member payload metadata.",
      "confidence": 0.82,
      "faang_parallel": "Android's APK verifier history is the relevant lesson: validators and consumers must agree byte-for-byte on container interpretation, or malformed containers become bypass material.",
      "metaphor": "The checksum is the tamper seal on the envelope. Reading the address before checking the seal lets a forged envelope steer the process.",
      "teachable_moment": "Pre-extract validation is only as strong as its parser equivalence with the extractor. Validate container integrity before trusting metadata.",
      "connection": "This is the same class of issue as archive-slip defenses: path checks are necessary, but parser disagreement can reopen the door."
    },
    {
      "id": "F-003",
      "title": "Global PAX path override is rejected for all normal archives",
      "severity": "LOW",
      "category": "compatibility",
      "file": "packages/protocol/collection/src/harness/archive.ts:338",
      "description": "Global PAX path/linkpath overrides are merged into every subsequent member, so a valid archive using a global PAX record with unrelated keys is fine, but any global path/linkpath makes every member share an effective path and fail. That is stricter than tar semantics and may reject archives produced by tools that emit global path metadata.",
      "suggestion": "If this strictness is intentional, document that global PAX path/linkpath records are unsupported. Otherwise, handle global records according to the target extractor behavior or explicitly reject them at the global header rather than applying them repeatedly.",
      "confidence": 0.66,
      "faang_parallel": "Bazel's remote cache compatibility work leans hard on documenting stricter-than-spec behavior so producers know which artifacts are portable.",
      "metaphor": "This is like a hotel giving every future guest the same room number because one lobby note mentioned a room.",
      "teachable_moment": "Strictness is fine when it is explicit. Undocumented strictness becomes accidental incompatibility.",
      "connection": "The broader pattern is protocol design: unsupported features should be rejected at the boundary where they appear, not after transformation makes the error look like something else."
    },
    {
      "id": "F-004",
      "title": "Isolated build avoids trusting checkout dist",
      "severity": "PRAISE",
      "category": "supply-chain",
      "file": "packages/protocol/collection/scripts/lib/isolated-harness.mjs:54",
      "description": "The pack and verify CLIs compile the harness from a fresh staging copy when TypeScript is available, and the tests include a poisoned checkout dist probe. This is a strong control for preventing stale or tampered generated output from influencing artifact creation.",
      "suggestion": "Keep this invariant covered by both the unit test and CI compatibility script.",
      "confidence": 0.98,
      "faang_parallel": "Chrome's release infrastructure similarly separates source truth from generated artifacts to reduce stale-build and supply-chain risk.",
      "metaphor": "You are baking from the recipe in a clean kitchen, not trusting a cake someone left on the counter.",
      "teachable_moment": "Generated output is a cache, not authority. Rebuilding from source inside the harness is the right default for provenance-sensitive tooling.",
      "connection": "This supports the PR's central compatibility goal: consumers can trust the harness behavior without trusting incidental local build state."
    },
    {
      "id": "F-005",
      "title": "Archive preflight covers high-risk tar member classes",
      "severity": "PRAISE",
      "category": "security",
      "file": "packages/protocol/collection/src/harness/archive.ts:538",
      "description": "The preflight rejects non-file members, link targets, path escapes, duplicate effective names, case collisions, and NFC collisions before extraction. The negative fixtures exercise PAX and GNU path override behavior, which is exactly where archive verification commonly drifts.",
      "suggestion": "Add checksum validation to complete this boundary, but the member-set model itself is sound.",
      "confidence": 0.94,
      "faang_parallel": "Docker and Kubernetes image handling both learned that archive member policy must be explicit before unpacking, especially around links and path normalization.",
      "metaphor": "This is a bouncer checking IDs, duplicate names, side doors, and fake badges before anyone enters the venue.",
      "teachable_moment": "Archive security is mostly about refusing ambiguity before extraction. This implementation already covers many of the dangerous ambiguity classes.",
      "connection": "Once checksum validation lands, this becomes a coherent layered boundary: container integrity, member identity, then extraction."
    }
  ]
}
```
<!-- bridge-findings-end -->

## Callouts

[Security] The archive preflight model is notably disciplined. Rejecting duplicate effective names, Unicode normalization collisions, link targets, and path escapes before extraction shows mature threat modeling.

[Quality] The isolated harness design is the strongest part of the PR. It encodes a valuable principle: compatibility artifacts should be produced from declared source, not whatever generated files happen to exist in the checkout.

[Test Coverage] The poisoned-dist probe is excellent test intent. After the cleanup trap fix, it will be a high-signal regression guard rather than a possible source of state leakage.

*Reviewed with: unknown v0.0.0*

## Summary
Verdict: `COMMENT`. The harness is thoughtfully shaped around strictness and artifact integrity, with especially strong archive metadata handling; the main concern is resource bounding around untrusted compressed inputs. Compatibility infrastructure becomes supply-chain infrastructure quickly, so size limits and documented trust boundaries deserve first-class treatment.

[Quality] The PR shows a clear compatibility-contract mindset. The next step is making resource budgets as explicit as schema rules, so future consumers inherit both correctness and operational safety.

## Summary
Verdict: `REQUEST_CHANGES`. The harness work shows strong security instincts around archive verification, but the root install hook creates a high-risk operational dependency on external network state during ordinary installs.

The architectural theme here is supply-chain boundaries: verifier code is doing the right thing by distrusting artifacts, while package/install plumbing needs the same discipline. Google’s SRE practice treats builds and installs as reproducible systems, not conveniences; this PR is close, but the install path currently has too much ambient authority.

## Summary

Verdict: `REQUEST_CHANGES`. The harness shows serious care around artifact verification, especially archive preflight and strict JSON handling, but the provenance path currently allows artifacts to claim a different source than the bytes being packed. The install-time network clone is also too operationally risky for a root lifecycle hook.

This PR is strongest where it treats compatibility artifacts as hostile inputs. It needs the same discipline on provenance and install behavior: identity metadata is part of the trust boundary, not decoration.
